concepts: Sine and cosine rules: sides, angles and ratios of cosines
questions.question: With usual notation, if in a $\triangle ABC$, $\frac{b+c}{11}=\frac{c+a}{12}=\frac{a+b}{13}$; then prove that $\frac{\cos A}{7}=\frac{\cos B}{19}=\frac{\cos C}{25}$.
questions.key_idea: Turn the three sums into $a:b:c=7:6:5$, then evaluate each cosine with the cosine rule.
solution: Adding the three: $2(a+b+c)=36k$, so $a+b+c=18k$.
Subtracting each given sum from $18k$: $a=18k-11k=7k$, $b=18k-12k=6k$, $c=18k-13k=5k$.
Hence $\frac{\cos A}{7}=\frac{\cos B}{19}=\frac{\cos C}{25}\ \left(=\frac1{35}\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops after writing the three cosine-rule formulas with the substituted squares; it never evaluates the cosines or forms the ratio that has to be proved. Steps 4-8 were added; the PDF's set-up (a = 7k, b = 6k, c = 5k) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Projection formulas $a=b\cos C+c\cos B$ etc. form a linear system in the cosines; $(7,19,25)$ solves it up to a common factor.
solution: With $a=7,\ b=6,\ c=5$ (scale $k$ cancels) the projection formulas are $7=6\cos C+5\cos B$, $6=5\cos A+7\cos C$, $5=7\cos B+6\cos A$.
Put $\cos A=7t$, $\cos B=19t$, $\cos C=25t$. The first gives $7=150t+95t=245t$, so $t=\frac1{35}$.
The second gives $6=35t+175t=210t$, so $t=\frac1{35}$; the third gives $5=133t+42t=175t$, so $t=\frac1{35}$ - all three agree.
The coefficient determinant $\begin{vmatrix}0&5&6\\5&0&7\\6&7&0\end{vmatrix}=420\neq0$, so the system has exactly one solution; hence $(\cos A,\cos B,\cos C)=\frac1{35}(7,19,25)$.
Therefore $\frac{\cos A}7=\frac{\cos B}{19}=\frac{\cos C}{25}$.

useful_results: If $\frac{b+c}p=\frac{c+a}q=\frac{a+b}r=k$ then $a=\frac{q+r-p}2k$, $b=\frac{p+r-q}2k$, $c=\frac{p+q-r}2k$ (here $p,q,r=11,12,13$ give $7k,6k,5k$).
$\cos A:\cos B:\cos C=a\left(b^2+c^2-a^2\right):b\left(c^2+a^2-b^2\right):c\left(a^2+b^2-c^2\right)$, because $\cos A=\frac{a\left(b^2+c^2-a^2\right)}{2abc}$; here $84:228:300=7:19:25$.
Projection formulas $a=b\cos C+c\cos B$, $b=c\cos A+a\cos C$, $c=a\cos B+b\cos A$ hold in every triangle and let you verify or solve for cosines without squares.

concepts: Angle bisector theorem and length of an angle bisector
Cosine rule and area of a triangle
questions.question: Given a triangle $ABC$ with $AB=2$ and $AC=1$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. If $AD=BD$ and $\Delta$ is the area of triangle $ABC$, then find the value of $12\Delta^2$.
questions.key_idea: $AD=BD$ turns the bisector-length formula into $\cos\frac A2=\frac a2$; comparing with the cosine rule gives $a^2=3$.
solution: $AB=2$, $AC=1$, $BC=a$. By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{CD}{DB}=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac12$, so $CD=\frac a3$ and $BD=\frac{2a}3$.
Length of the bisector from $A$: $AD=\frac{2bc\cos\frac A2}{b+c}=\frac{2\cdot2\cdot1}{3}\cos\frac A2=\frac43\cos\frac A2$.
Given $AD=BD$: $\frac43\cos\frac A2=\frac{2a}3$, so $\cos\frac A2=\frac a2$.
Then $\cos A=2\cos^2\frac A2-1=\frac{a^2}2-1$.
By the cosine rule, $\cos A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}=\frac{1+4-a^2}{4}=\frac{5-a^2}4$.
Equate: $\frac{a^2}2-1=\frac{5-a^2}4\Rightarrow2a^2-4=5-a^2\Rightarrow a^2=3$.
Then $\cos A=\frac{5-3}4=\frac12$, so $A=60^\circ$ and $\sin A=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
$\Delta=\frac12bc\sin A=\frac12\cdot2\cdot1\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $12\Delta^2=12\cdot\frac34=9$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes cos A = (5 - a^2)/3. The denominator is 2bc = 4, so cos A = (5 - a^2)/4. With /3 the equation would give a^2 = 16/5, not the a^2 = 3 that the PDF uses next; the typo is corrected, the answer 9 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $AD=BD$ makes $\triangle ABD$ isosceles, so $B=\frac A2$; the sine rule then gives $A$ directly.
solution: In $\triangle ABD$, $AD=BD$ gives $\angle DBA=\angle DAB=\frac A2$, so $B=\frac A2$ and $C=\pi-\frac{3A}2$.
Sine rule: $\frac c{\sin C}=\frac b{\sin B}$, so $\frac2{\sin\frac{3A}2}=\frac1{\sin\frac A2}$.
$\sin\frac{3A}2=2\sin\frac A2\Rightarrow3-4\sin^2\frac A2=2\Rightarrow\sin^2\frac A2=\frac14$.
$\frac A2=30^\circ$ (as $\frac A2<90^\circ$), so $A=60^\circ$.
$\Delta=\frac12\cdot2\cdot1\cdot\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $12\Delta^2=9$.

useful_results: $AD=BD$ with $D$ on $BC$ forces $\angle B=\frac A2$: an equal-segment condition becomes an angle relation, after which the sine rule finishes the question.
Angle bisector from $A$: $BD:DC=c:b$ and length $l_A=\frac{2bc\cos\frac A2}{b+c}$.
$A=2B\iff a^2=b(b+c)$; here $a^2=1\cdot(1+2)=3$ agrees with the answer.

concepts: Sine rule and circumradius
Sum and difference of sines: sum to product
questions.question: In a triangle $ABC$, let the angles $A,B,C$ be in G.P. with common ratio $2$. If the circumradius of triangle $ABC$ is $2$, then find the value of $\left(b^{-1}+c^{-1}-a^{-1}\right)$.
questions.key_idea: Write the sides as $2R\sin$ of the angles; with $\sin\frac{4\pi}7=\sin\frac{3\pi}7$ the sum $\frac1{\sin B}+\frac1{\sin C}$ collapses to $\frac1{\sin A}$.
solution: Let $A=\alpha$, $B=2\alpha$, $C=4\alpha$ and $R=2$. $A+B+C=\pi\Rightarrow7\alpha=\pi$, so $\alpha=\frac\pi7$.
So $\angle A=\frac\pi7$, $\angle B=\frac{2\pi}7$ and $\angle C=\frac{4\pi}7$.
Sine rule: $\frac a{\sin A}=\frac b{\sin B}=\frac c{\sin C}=2R$, so $\frac1b+\frac1c-\frac1a=\frac1{2R}\left[\frac1{\sin B}+\frac1{\sin C}-\frac1{\sin A}\right]$.
$\frac1{\sin B}+\frac1{\sin C}=\frac{\sin B+\sin C}{\sin B\sin C}=\frac{2\sin\frac{B+C}2\cos\frac{B-C}2}{\sin B\sin C}$.
Here $\frac{B+C}2=\frac{3\pi}7$ and $\cos\frac{B-C}2=\cos\frac\pi7$, so the expression is $\frac{2\sin\frac{3\pi}7\cos\frac\pi7}{\sin\frac{2\pi}7\sin\frac{4\pi}7}$.
$\sin\frac{4\pi}7=\sin\frac{3\pi}7$, so $\sin\frac{3\pi}7$ cancels: $\frac{2\cos\frac\pi7}{\sin\frac{2\pi}7}=\frac{2\cos\frac\pi7}{2\sin\frac\pi7\cos\frac\pi7}=\frac1{\sin\frac\pi7}$.
Hence $\frac1b+\frac1c-\frac1a=\frac1{2R}\left[\frac1{\sin\frac\pi7}-\frac1{\sin\frac\pi7}\right]=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes angle C = 9*pi/7, which would make A + B + C = 12*pi/7. The correct value is C = 4*pi/7 (the PDF's later lines already use 4*pi/7 and 3*pi/7). Corrected; the answer 0 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The sides are the side and the two diagonals of a regular heptagon, and Ptolemy's theorem gives $\frac1a=\frac1b+\frac1c$.
solution: In a regular heptagon $P_1P_2\dots P_7$ inscribed in a circle of radius $R$: the side is $p=2R\sin\frac\pi7$, the short diagonal $P_1P_3=q=2R\sin\frac{2\pi}7$ and the long diagonal $P_1P_4=r=2R\sin\frac{3\pi}7$.
The triangle's sides are $a=2R\sin\frac\pi7=p$, $b=2R\sin\frac{2\pi}7=q$ and $c=2R\sin\frac{4\pi}7=2R\sin\frac{3\pi}7=r$.
Ptolemy on the cyclic quadrilateral $P_1P_2P_3P_5$: diagonals $P_1P_3=q$ and $P_2P_5=r$; sides $P_1P_2=p$, $P_2P_3=p$, $P_3P_5=q$, $P_5P_1=r$. So $qr=pq+pr$.
Dividing by $pqr$: $\frac1p=\frac1r+\frac1q$, that is $\frac1a=\frac1b+\frac1c$.
Hence $\frac1b+\frac1c-\frac1a=0$, whatever the circumradius is (in particular for $R=2$).

useful_results: $\frac1{\sin\frac\pi7}=\frac1{\sin\frac{2\pi}7}+\frac1{\sin\frac{3\pi}7}$; geometrically, in a regular heptagon with side $p$ and diagonals $q<r$ we have $\frac1p=\frac1q+\frac1r$ (Ptolemy).

A triangle with angles $\frac\pi7,\frac{2\pi}7,\frac{4\pi}7$ is the 'heptagonal triangle'; its sides satisfy $\frac1a=\frac1b+\frac1c$ for every circumradius, so the value $R=2$ in the question is a distractor.
When angles add to $\pi$, use $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$ to make sines coincide: $\sin\frac{4\pi}7=\sin\frac{3\pi}7$.

questions.question: For any triangle $ABC$, if $B=3C$, show that $\cos C=\sqrt{\frac{b+c}{4c}}$ and $\sin\frac A2=\frac{b-c}{2c}$.
questions.key_idea: $\frac bc=\frac{\sin3C}{\sin C}=4\cos^2C-1$, and $\frac A2=\frac\pi2-2C$ makes $\sin\frac A2=\cos2C$.
solution: $B=3C\Rightarrow\sin B=\sin3C$, so $\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}=\frac{\sin3C}{\sin C}=3-4\sin^2C$, and by the sine rule this equals $\frac bc$.
$3-4\sin^2C=\frac bc\Rightarrow3-4\left(1-\cos^2C\right)=\frac bc$.
$4\cos^2C-1=\frac bc\Rightarrow4\cos^2C=\frac{b+c}c$.
$\cos C=\sqrt{\frac{b+c}{4c}}$ (positive: $A=\pi-4C>0$ gives $C<\frac\pi4$).
$A+B+C=\pi\Rightarrow A=\pi-4C\Rightarrow\frac A2=\frac\pi2-2C$.
$\sin\frac A2=\cos2C=2\cos^2C-1=\frac{2(b+c)}{4c}-1=\frac{b+c-2c}{2c}=\frac{b-c}{2c}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $b=2R\sin B$, $c=2R\sin C$ and convert $b+c$ and $b-c$ with sum-to-product formulas.
solution: $b+c=2R(\sin3C+\sin C)=2R\cdot2\sin2C\cos C=8R\sin C\cos^2C$.
Since $c=2R\sin C$, this is $b+c=4c\cos^2C$, so $\cos C=\sqrt{\frac{b+c}{4c}}$ (positive because $C<\frac\pi4$).
$b-c=2R(\sin3C-\sin C)=2R\cdot2\cos2C\sin C=2c\cos2C$.
Since $\frac A2=\frac\pi2-2C$, $\sin\frac A2=\cos2C=\frac{b-c}{2c}$.

useful_results: $\frac{\sin3\theta}{\sin\theta}=3-4\sin^2\theta=4\cos^2\theta-1$: if $B=3C$ then $\frac bc=4\cos^2C-1$.
If $B=nC$ conditions are best handled with the sine rule $\frac bc=\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}$ and a multiple-angle identity.
Related standard fact: $B=2C\iff b^2=c(a+c)$ (and $\frac bc=2\cos C$).

Right triangle inside a triangle: perpendicular median and side
questions.question: In a triangle $ABC$, $BD$ is a median. If $l(BD)=\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot l(AB)$ and $\angle DBC=\frac\pi2$, determine $\angle ABC$.
questions.key_idea: The right angle at $B$ in $\triangle DBC$ links $a,b,c$; with the median formula it gives $4b^2=7c^2$ and then $\angle ABD$.
solution: Let $AB=c$, $BC=a$, $CA=b$; $D$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $BD=\frac{\sqrt3}4c$.
Median formula: $BD=\frac12\sqrt{2a^2+2c^2-b^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}4c$, so $2a^2+2c^2-b^2=\frac{3c^2}4$ ...(1)
In $\triangle DBC$ the angle at $B$ is $90^\circ$, with $DC=\frac b2$: $a^2=\frac{b^2}4-\frac{3c^2}{16}$.
Put this in (1): $2\left(\frac{b^2}4-\frac{3c^2}{16}\right)+2c^2-b^2=\frac{3c^2}4$.
$\frac{b^2}2-\frac{3c^2}8+2c^2-b^2-\frac{3c^2}4=0\Rightarrow-\frac{b^2}2+\frac{7c^2}8=0\Rightarrow4b^2=7c^2$.
Let $\theta=\angle ABD$. In $\triangle ABD$ (with $AD=\frac b2$): $\cos\theta=\frac{c^2+\frac{3c^2}{16}-\frac{b^2}4}{2\cdot c\cdot\frac{\sqrt3c}4}=\frac{19c^2-4b^2}{8\sqrt3c^2}$.
With $4b^2=7c^2$: $\cos\theta=\frac{12c^2}{8\sqrt3c^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $\theta=30^\circ$.
$\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle DBC=30^\circ+90^\circ=120^\circ$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Double the median: extend $BD$ to $E$ with $DE=BD$; $ABCE$ is a parallelogram and $\triangle ABE$ is right-angled at $E$.
solution: Extend $BD$ to $E$ so that $DE=BD$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ of $ABCE$ bisect each other at $D$, so $ABCE$ is a parallelogram: $AE\parallel BC$ and $BE=2BD=\frac{\sqrt3}2c$.
$AE\parallel BC$ and $BE$ is a transversal, so $\angle AEB=\angle EBC=\angle DBC=90^\circ$.
In the right triangle $AEB$: $\cos\angle ABE=\frac{BE}{AB}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt3}2c}c=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $\angle ABE=30^\circ$.
$\angle ABC=\angle ABE+\angle EBC=30^\circ+90^\circ=120^\circ$.

useful_results: Doubling a median: extending the median $BD$ to $E$ with $DE=BD$ makes $ABCE$ a parallelogram with $BE=2BD$ and $AE=BC$.
Median length: $m_b=\frac12\sqrt{2a^2+2c^2-b^2}$ (Apollonius).
A right angle between a median and a side turns into a right angle of the parallelogram $ABCE$, so the angle at $B$ is $90^\circ+\arccos\frac{BE}{AB}$.

questions.question: In an isosceles $\triangle ABC$ ($AB=AC$), if the altitudes intersect on the inscribed circle, then find the secant of the vertical angle $A$.
questions.key_idea: The orthocentre on the axis lies on the incircle at distance $2r$ from $D$, so $AH+2r=AD$ with $AH=2R\cos A$.
solution: Let $O$ be the orthocentre and $D$ the foot of the altitude from $A$, which is also the point where the incircle touches $BC$. $O$ lies on $AD$ and on the incircle, so $OD=2r$.
$OA=2R\cos A$ and $AD=\frac a2\cot\frac A2$; since $OA+OD=AD$: $2r+2R\cos A=\frac a2\cot\frac A2$.
Put $r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$ and $a=2R\sin A$: $8\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2+2\cos A=\sin A\cot\frac A2=2\cos^2\frac A2$.
$2\cos^2\frac A2=\cos A+1$, so $\cos A=1-8\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$.
Since $B=C$ and $A+B+C=\pi$, $\frac B2=\frac C2=\frac\pi4-\frac A4$, so $\cos A=1-8\sin\frac A2\sin^2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac A4\right)$.
$\sin^2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac A4\right)=\frac12\left(\cos\frac A4-\sin\frac A4\right)^2=\frac12\left(1-\sin\frac A2\right)$, so $1-2\sin^2\frac A2=1-4\sin\frac A2\left(1-\sin\frac A2\right)$.
$-2\sin^2\frac A2=-4\sin\frac A2+4\sin^2\frac A2\Rightarrow6\sin\frac A2=4$, so $\sin\frac A2=\frac23$.
$\cos A=1-2\sin^2\frac A2=1-2\cdot\frac49=\frac19$, so $\sec A=9$.
questions.correction_note: In the line 'cos A = 1 - 8 sin(B/2) sin^2(pi/4 - A/4)' the PDF has sin(B/2) where sin(A/2) is meant (the next lines use sin(A/2)). Corrected; the PDF's own steps after that (sin(A/2) = 2 - 2 sin(A/2) etc.) are written out in full in the clean form shown. Answer 9 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates with the axis as the $y$-axis: put $t=\tan\frac A2$; the orthocentre height $t^2$ must equal $2r$.
solution: Take $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,1)$, $B=(-t,0)$, $C=(t,0)$ where $t=\tan\frac A2$. The orthocentre lies on the axis.
The altitude from $B$ is perpendicular to $AC$, which has direction $(t,-1)$: its equation is $t(x+t)-y=0$, so it meets the axis at $H=(0,t^2)$.
Area $=t$ and semi-perimeter $s=t+\sqrt{1+t^2}$, so $r=\frac{t}{t+\sqrt{1+t^2}}$; the incircle meets the axis at $(0,0)$ and $(0,2r)$.
$t\sqrt{1+t^2}=2-t^2$; squaring, $t^2+t^4=4-4t^2+t^4$, so $t^2=\frac45$ (and $2-t^2>0$ holds).

useful_results: Distances from the orthocentre: $AH=2R\cos A$ and $HD=2R\cos B\cos C$ (acute triangle); inradius $r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$.
In an isosceles triangle the orthocentre, incentre and circumcentre all lie on the axis; the incircle meets the axis at $D$ and at the point $2r$ above it.

Using $t=\tan\frac A2$ with altitude $1$ makes every length rational in $t$: $a=2t$, $\text{leg}=\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $H=t^2$. The condition 'orthocentre on the incircle' holds exactly when $\cos A=\frac19$ ($A\approx83.6^\circ$).

concepts: Altitude and median from a vertex: sine rule in sub-triangles
questions.question: Find the angles of a triangle in which the altitude and the median drawn from the same vertex divide the angle at that vertex into $3$ equal parts.
questions.answer: $30^\circ,\ 60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ (the angle at the vertex is $90^\circ$)
questions.key_idea: Write $A=3\alpha$, apply the sine rule in $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle AEC$ to get $AE$ two ways, and equate.
solution: Let $A=3\alpha$ with $\angle BAD=\angle DAE=\angle EAC=\alpha$, where $AD\perp BC$ and $E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $BE=EC=\frac a2$.
In $\triangle ABE$: $\angle BAE=2\alpha$ and $\angle ABE=90^\circ-\alpha$, so $\frac{a/2}{\sin2\alpha}=\frac{AE}{\sin(90^\circ-\alpha)}$.
$AE=\frac{a\cos\alpha}{2\sin2\alpha}=\frac a{4\sin\alpha}$ ...(1)
In $\triangle AEC$: $\angle EAC=\alpha$ and $\angle ACE=90^\circ-2\alpha$, so $\frac{a/2}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{AE}{\sin(90^\circ-2\alpha)}$.
$AE=\frac{a\cos2\alpha}{2\sin\alpha}$ ...(2)
From (1) and (2): $\frac a{4\sin\alpha}=\frac{a\cos2\alpha}{2\sin\alpha}\Rightarrow\cos2\alpha=\frac12$.
$2\alpha=\frac\pi3$ ($0<2\alpha<\pi$), so $\alpha=\frac\pi6$ and $A=3\alpha=\frac\pi2$.
$B=90^\circ-\alpha=60^\circ$ and $C=90^\circ-2\alpha=30^\circ$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The altitude bisects $\angle BAE$, so $\triangle ABE$ is isosceles with $D$ the midpoint of $BE$; the angle bisector theorem in $\triangle ADC$ then gives $\cos2\alpha$.
solution: $AD$ bisects $\angle BAE$ and $AD\perp BE$, so $\triangle ABE$ is isosceles with $AB=AE$ and $BD=DE=x$.
$E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $EC=BE=2x$.
In the right triangle $ADC$, $AE$ bisects $\angle DAC=2\alpha$, so by the angle bisector theorem $\frac{AD}{AC}=\frac{DE}{EC}=\frac x{2x}=\frac12$.
But $\frac{AD}{AC}=\cos\angle DAC=\cos2\alpha$, so $\cos2\alpha=\frac12$, $2\alpha=60^\circ$, $\alpha=30^\circ$.
Hence $A=90^\circ$, $B=90^\circ-\alpha=60^\circ$ and $C=90^\circ-2\alpha=30^\circ$.

useful_results: If the altitude from $A$ also bisects $\angle BAE$, then $AB=AE$ and the altitude is the perpendicular bisector of $BE$.
Angle bisector theorem in a right triangle: if $AE$ bisects $\angle DAC$ in the right triangle $ADC$, then $\frac{DE}{EC}=\frac{AD}{AC}=\cos\angle DAC$.

In a right triangle ($A=90^\circ$) the median to the hypotenuse equals half of it, so the median and altitude from $A$ automatically make equal angles $\angle BAD=\angle EAC$; the trisection fixes $B=60^\circ$.

concepts: Sine rule, circumradius and right triangle

questions.question: The ratios of the lengths of the sides $BC$ and $AC$ of $\triangle ABC$ to the radius of the circumscribed circle are equal to $2$ and $\frac32$ respectively. If the ratio of the lengths of the bisectors of the interior angles $B$ and $C$ is $\frac{\alpha\left(\sqrt\alpha-1\right)}{\beta\sqrt\gamma}$ where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in N$, then find the value of $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$.
questions.key_idea: $\sin A=\frac a{2R}=1$ makes $A=90^\circ$; each bisector is then the hypotenuse of a right triangle with leg $AB$ or $AC$.
solution: Let $BC=a$, $AC=b$ with $\frac aR=2$ and $\frac bR=\frac32$. Sine rule $a=2R\sin A$ gives $2\sin A=2$, so $\sin A=1$ and $A=\frac\pi2$.
$\sin B=\frac b{2R}=\frac34$. With $A=90^\circ$: $a=2R$ is the hypotenuse, $b=\frac{3R}2$ and $c=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}=\sqrt{4R^2-\frac{9R^2}4}=\frac{\sqrt7}2R$.
The bisector from $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$ with $AD=AC\cdot\frac{AB}{AB+BC}=\frac{bc}{a+c}=\frac{3\sqrt7R}{2\left(4+\sqrt7\right)}$.
The bisector from $C$ meets $AB$ at $E$ with $AE=\frac{bc}{a+b}=\frac{3\sqrt7R}{14}$.
Right angle at $A$: $BD=\sqrt{AB^2+AD^2}=\frac{2\sqrt7R}{\sqrt7+1}$ and $CE=\sqrt{AC^2+AE^2}=\frac{3\sqrt2R}{\sqrt7}$.
$\frac{BD}{CE}=\frac{2\sqrt7}{\sqrt7+1}\cdot\frac{\sqrt7}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{14}{3\sqrt2\left(\sqrt7+1\right)}=\frac{14\left(\sqrt7-1\right)}{3\sqrt2\cdot6}=\frac{7\left(\sqrt7-1\right)}{9\sqrt2}$.
So $\alpha=7$, $\beta=9$, $\gamma=2$ and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=18$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In a right triangle the bisector from an acute vertex is $\frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\cos(\text{half-angle})}$, so the ratio comes from half-angle cosines.
solution: Take $R=2$: $a=4$, $b=3$, $c=\sqrt7$ with $A=90^\circ$; $\cos B=\frac ca=\frac{\sqrt7}4$ and $\cos C=\frac ba=\frac34$.
In the right triangle $ABD$ (right angle at $A$) $BD=\frac{AB}{\cos\frac B2}=\frac c{\cos\frac B2}$; likewise $CE=\frac b{\cos\frac C2}$.
$\frac{BD}{CE}=\frac cb\cdot\frac{\cos\frac C2}{\cos\frac B2}=\frac{\sqrt7}3\sqrt{\frac{1+\frac34}{1+\frac{\sqrt7}4}}=\frac{\sqrt7}3\sqrt{\frac7{4+\sqrt7}}=\frac7{3\sqrt{4+\sqrt7}}$.

$\left(\sqrt7+1\right)^2=2\left(4+\sqrt7\right)$, so $\sqrt{4+\sqrt7}=\frac{\sqrt7+1}{\sqrt2}$ and the ratio is $\frac{7\sqrt2}{3\left(\sqrt7+1\right)}=\frac{7\sqrt2\left(\sqrt7-1\right)}{18}=\frac{7\left(\sqrt7-1\right)}{9\sqrt2}$.
Hence $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(7,9,2)$ and the sum is $18$.

useful_results: $\frac a{2R}=\sin A=1$ means $a$ is a diameter and $A=90^\circ$: a side equal to $2R$ signals a right angle opposite it.
In a triangle right-angled at $A$, the bisector of $B$ has length $\frac{AB}{\cos\frac B2}$ and the bisector of $C$ has length $\frac{AC}{\cos\frac C2}$.
Angle bisector foot: the bisector from $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$ with $AD=\frac{bc}{a+c}$.
Denesting: $\sqrt{p+\sqrt q}=\sqrt{\frac{p+d}2}+\sqrt{\frac{p-d}2}$ with $d=\sqrt{p^2-q}$; here $\sqrt{4+\sqrt7}=\frac{\sqrt7+1}{\sqrt2}$ ($d=3$).

concepts: Circumradius of triangles formed by the diagonals of a rhombus
Properties of a rhombus and half-angle formulas
questions.question: $ABCD$ is a rhombus. The circumradii of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$ are $12.5$ and $25$ respectively. Find the area of the rhombus.
questions.key_idea: The sine rule in $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$ gives $BD:AC=1:2$; then $\tan\frac{\theta_1}2=\frac{BD}{AC}$ fixes $\sin\theta_1$.
solution: Let $BD=p$, $AC=q$, $\theta_1=\angle BAD$ and $\theta_2=\angle ADC$; adjacent angles of a rhombus satisfy $\theta_1+\theta_2=\pi$.
In $\triangle ABD$: $\frac p{\sin\theta_1}=2R_1=25$, so $p=25\sin\theta_1$.
In $\triangle ACD$: $\frac q{\sin\theta_2}=2R_2=50$, so $q=50\sin\theta_2$.
$\sin\theta_2=\sin(\pi-\theta_1)=\sin\theta_1$, so $\frac pq=\frac{25}{50}=\frac12$.
The diagonals meet at $M$ at right angles. In $\triangle AMD$: $\frac{\theta_1}2+\frac{\theta_2}2=\frac\pi2$ and $\tan\frac{\theta_1}2=\frac{DM}{AM}=\frac{p/2}{q/2}=\frac pq=\frac12$.
$\sin\theta_1=\frac{2\tan\frac{\theta_1}2}{1+\tan^2\frac{\theta_1}2}=\frac{1}{1+\frac14}=\frac45$.
$p=25\cdot\frac45=20$ and $q=2p=40$.
Area of the rhombus $=\frac12pq=\frac12\cdot20\cdot40=400$ sq. units.
questions.correction_note: For triangle ABD the PDF writes q/sin(theta_1) = 2R; the side opposite angle theta_1 in triangle ABD is BD = p (the PDF's next line p = 2R sin(theta_1) uses it correctly). Corrected to p/sin(theta_1) = 2R. All values and the answer 400 are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: In an isosceles triangle $R=\frac{\text{equal side}^2}{2\times\text{altitude}}$; both circumradii then share the same $a^2$.
solution: Let the half-diagonals be $u=AM$ and $v=DM$, so $AC=2u$, $BD=2v$ and the side is $a$ with $a^2=u^2+v^2$.
$\triangle ABD$ is isosceles ($AB=AD=a$) with base $2v$ and altitude $AM=u$: $R_1=\frac{abc}{4\Delta}=\frac{a\cdot a\cdot2v}{4uv}=\frac{a^2}{2u}$.
$\triangle ACD$ is isosceles ($DA=DC=a$) with base $2u$ and altitude $DM=v$: $R_2=\frac{a^2}{2v}$.
Area $=\frac12(2u)(2v)=2uv=2\cdot20\cdot10=400$.

useful_results: Isosceles triangle with equal sides $a$ and altitude $h$ to the base: $R=\frac{a^2}{2h}$.
In a rhombus of side $a$: $R_{ABD}=\frac{a^2}{AC}$ and $R_{ACD}=\frac{a^2}{BD}$, so $\frac{R_{ABD}}{R_{ACD}}=\frac{BD}{AC}$ (here $\frac{12.5}{25}=\frac12$).
Then $a^2=\frac{AC^2+BD^2}4$ and area $=\frac12AC\cdot BD$; here $a^2=500$, $AC=40$, $BD=20$.

concepts: Cotangent ratio identity: cot C/(cot A + cot B) in terms of sides
questions.question: In a triangle $ABC$, if $a^2+b^2=101c^2$, then find the value of $\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}$.
questions.key_idea: $\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2c^2}$ in every triangle.
solution: $\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{\cos C}{\sin C}\cdot\frac{\sin A\sin B}{\cos A\sin B+\cos B\sin A}$.
$=\frac{\cos C\sin A\sin B}{\sin C\sin(A+B)}=\frac{\cos C\sin A\sin B}{\sin^2C}$, since $\sin(A+B)=\sin C$.
Cosine rule and sine rule: $\cos C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$, $\sin A\sin B=\frac{ab}{4R^2}$, $\sin^2C=\frac{c^2}{4R^2}$.
$\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\cdot\frac{ab}{4R^2}\cdot\frac{4R^2}{c^2}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2c^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cot A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}$ for each angle; the common factor $4\Delta$ cancels at once.
solution: In any triangle $\cot A=\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}\cdot\frac{bc}{2\Delta}=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}$, and similarly for $B$ and $C$.
$\cot A+\cot B=\frac{(b^2+c^2-a^2)+(c^2+a^2-b^2)}{4\Delta}=\frac{2c^2}{4\Delta}$.
$\cot C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{4\Delta}$, so $\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2c^2}$.

useful_results: In any triangle $\cot A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}$, hence $\cot A+\cot B+\cot C=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta}$ and $\cot A+\cot B=\frac{c^2}{2\Delta}$.
$\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2c^2}$; so if $a^2+b^2=kc^2$ the ratio is $\frac{k-1}2$.
Also $\cot A\cot B+\cot B\cot C+\cot C\cot A=1$ in every triangle.

concepts: Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles, area and cosine rule
questions.question: The two adjacent sides of a cyclic quadrilateral are $2$ and $5$ and the angle between them is $60^\circ$. If the area of the quadrilateral is $4\sqrt3$, find the remaining two sides.
questions.key_idea: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$; area and the common diagonal give $ab=6$ and $a^2+b^2=13$.
solution: Let $ABCD$ be cyclic with $DA=2$, $DC=5$, $\angle ADC=60^\circ$; the unknown sides are $AB=a$ and $BC=b$.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: $\angle ABC=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$.
Area $=[ADC]+[ABC]=\frac12\cdot2\cdot5\sin60^\circ+\frac12ab\sin120^\circ=\frac{5\sqrt3}2+\frac{\sqrt3}4ab=4\sqrt3$.
$\frac{\sqrt3}4ab=\frac{3\sqrt3}2\Rightarrow ab=6$.
Diagonal $AC$ from $\triangle ADC$: $AC^2=2^2+5^2-2\cdot2\cdot5\cos60^\circ=19$.
From $\triangle ABC$: $AC^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos120^\circ=a^2+b^2+ab$, so $a^2+b^2=19-6=13$.
The remaining sides are $3$ and $2$ (in either order): $\{a,b\}=\{3,2\}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's figure and working assume AB parallel to DC (a cyclic trapezoid), which the question does not give, and label an angle 30 degrees (it would be 60 degrees in an isosceles trapezoid); it finds only one arrangement (AB = 3, BC = 2). Rewritten using only the given data: opposite angles supplementary, area and the common diagonal. It shows that the other two sides are 3 and 2 in either order; the PDF's configuration is kept as the alternate (with the angle corrected). The answer 3 and 2 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: A cyclic trapezoid is isosceles: build $AB\parallel DC$ with $AD=BC=2$; the data fit it exactly (the PDF's picture, with the angle corrected).
solution: Take $ABCD$ with $AB\parallel DC$, $DC=5$, $AD=2$ and $\angle D=60^\circ$. A cyclic trapezoid is isosceles, so $BC=AD=2$ and $\angle C=60^\circ$.
Drop perpendiculars $AM$ and $BN$ on $DC$: $DM=NC=2\cos60^\circ=1$ and the height is $AM=2\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3$.
Area $=\frac12(AB+DC)\cdot AM=\frac12(3+5)\sqrt3=4\sqrt3$, exactly the given area.
So the remaining sides $3$ and $2$ realise the data (and the main solution shows they are the only possible pair of lengths).

useful_results: In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add to $180^\circ$, so the area splits as $\frac12xy\sin\theta+\frac12zw\sin\theta$ with the same $\sin\theta$.
Equate the two expressions for the common diagonal: $x^2+y^2-2xy\cos\theta=z^2+w^2+2zw\cos\theta$.
Brahmagupta's formula: area $=\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}$; check: sides $2,5,3,2$ give $s=6$ and $\sqrt{4\cdot1\cdot3\cdot4}=4\sqrt3$.

concepts: Tangent circles: distances between centres and the cosine rule
Arc length of the locus of a centre
questions.question: A point $O$ is situated on a circle of radius $R$ and with centre $O$, another circle of radius $\frac{3R}2$ is described. Inside the crescent shaped area intercepted between these circles, a circle of radius $\frac R8$ is placed. If the same circle moves in contact with the original circle of radius $R$, then find the length of the arc described by its centre in moving from one extreme position to the other.
questions.key_idea: The small circle's centre stays $\frac{7R}8$ from the centre of the original circle; the extreme positions touch the big circle, fixed by the cosine rule.
solution: Let $B$ be the centre of the original circle $C_2$ (radius $R$), $A$ the point $O$ on it (the centre of $C_1$ of radius $\frac{3R}2$), so $AB=R$. Let $C$ be the centre of the small circle in one extreme position and $\angle ABC=\theta$.
The small circle touches $C_1$ externally: $AC=\frac{3R}2+\frac R8=\frac{13R}8$. It touches $C_2$ internally: $BC=R-\frac R8=\frac{7R}8$.
In $\triangle ABC$: $\cos\theta=\frac{AB^2+BC^2-AC^2}{2\cdot AB\cdot BC}=\frac{R^2+\frac{49R^2}{64}-\frac{169R^2}{64}}{2\cdot R\cdot\frac{7R}8}$.
$\cos\theta=\frac{-\frac{56R^2}{64}}{\frac{7R^2}4}=-\frac12$, so $\theta=120^\circ$.
By symmetry the other extreme position $D$ has $\angle ABD=120^\circ$, on the other side of $AB$.
$\angle CBD=360^\circ-120^\circ-120^\circ=120^\circ=\frac{2\pi}3$.
The centre moves on the circle of radius $BC=\frac{7R}8$ about $B$, so the arc $CD=\frac{7R}8\cdot\frac{2\pi}3=\frac{7\pi R}{12}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 45R^2/64 for (7R/8)^2 (it is 49R^2/64; the PDF's next line, -56R^2/64, already uses 49), writes 'angle BDC = 120 deg' where angle CBD is meant, and gives the final arc as 7*pi*r/12 with a small r instead of R. Corrected; the answer 7*pi*R/12 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates: subtracting the two circle equations (radical axis of the two centre-loci) gives the $x$-coordinate of the centre at once.
solution: Take $B=(0,0)$ and $A=(R,0)$. The centre $C=(x,y)$ satisfies $x^2+y^2=\left(\frac{7R}8\right)^2$ (internal contact with $C_2$) and $(x-R)^2+y^2=\left(\frac{13R}8\right)^2$ (external contact with $C_1$).
Then $\cos\angle ABC=\frac{x}{7R/8}=-\frac12$, so $C$ lies in the direction $120^\circ$ from $BA$; the other extreme position is the mirror image at $-120^\circ$.
The two extreme directions differ by $360^\circ-240^\circ=120^\circ$ through the side away from $A$, which is the part of the circle of radius $\frac{7R}8$ lying in the crescent.
Arc length $=\frac{7R}8\cdot\frac{2\pi}3=\frac{7\pi R}{12}$.

useful_results: A circle of radius $\rho$ touching a fixed circle of radius $R$ internally has its centre at distance $R-\rho$ from the fixed centre; touching another circle (radius $r_1$) externally puts it at distance $r_1+\rho$ from that centre.

The extreme positions of a circle moving inside a region occur when it just touches the second boundary; the three centres form a triangle whose sides are all known, so the cosine rule gives the angle.
Arc length of the locus $=$ radius of the locus circle $\times$ the angle subtended at its centre: here $\frac{7R}8\times\frac{2\pi}3$.

concepts: Napier's analogy (tangent rule) and half-angle formulas
Area of a triangle
questions.question: If in a $\triangle ABC$, $a=6$, $b=3$ and $\cos(A-B)=\frac45$, then find its area.
questions.key_idea: $\cos(A-B)=\frac45$ gives $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac13$; Napier's analogy then gives $\cot\frac C2=1$, so $C=90^\circ$.
solution: $a=6$, $b=3$ and $\cos(A-B)=\frac45$. Since $a>b$, $A>B$ and $0<\frac{A-B}2<\frac\pi2$.
$2\cos^2\frac{A-B}2-1=\frac45\Rightarrow\cos^2\frac{A-B}2=\frac9{10}$, so $\cos\frac{A-B}2=\frac3{\sqrt{10}}$ and $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac13$.
Napier's analogy: $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2$, so $\frac13=\frac{6-3}{6+3}\cot\frac C2=\frac13\cot\frac C2$.
$\cot\frac C2=1\Rightarrow\frac C2=45^\circ$, so $C=90^\circ$.
Area $=\frac12ab\sin C=\frac12\cdot6\cdot3=9$ sq. unit.
questions.correction_note: Two lines of the PDF are garbled: '2cos^2((A-B)/2) = a/5' (it should be 9/5, since 2cos^2((A-B)/2) = 1 + 4/5) and 'cos((A-B)/2) = 3/sqrt10 = A/K' (the last equality is meaningless). The cleaned lines are shown; the method, the value C = 90 degrees and the answer 9 are as in the PDF.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $A=B+\delta$ and use $\sin A=2\sin B$ (from $a=2b$): the equation reduces to $\tan B=\frac12$, so $\tan A\tan B=1$.
solution: $A>B$; let $\delta=A-B$ with $\cos\delta=\frac45$, $\sin\delta=\frac35$. The sine rule with $a=2b$ gives $\sin A=2\sin B$.
$\sin(B+\delta)=2\sin B\Rightarrow\frac45\sin B+\frac35\cos B=2\sin B\Rightarrow3\cos B=6\sin B$, so $\tan B=\frac12$.
$\tan\delta=\frac34$, so $\tan A=\frac{\frac12+\frac34}{1-\frac12\cdot\frac34}=\frac{5/4}{5/8}=2$.
$\tan A\tan B=1$ with $A,B$ acute gives $A+B=90^\circ$, so $C=90^\circ$.
Area $=\frac12ab=\frac12\cdot6\cdot3=9$.

useful_results: Napier's analogy: $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2$; given two sides and $A-B$ it yields $C$ without finding $A$ or $B$.
If $A,B$ are acute and $\tan A\tan B=1$ then $A+B=90^\circ$, i.e. $C=90^\circ$.
$\cos(A-B)=\frac45$ with $a:b=2:1$ is the $3:4:5$-type configuration: the triangle is right-angled with legs $6$ and $3$ ($\tan A=2$).

concepts: Isosceles-triangle conditions: cosine rule, sine rule and half-angle tangents
questions.question: In a $\triangle ABC$, (i) $\frac a{\cos A}=\frac b{\cos B}$ (ii) $2\sin A\cos B=\sin C$ (iii) $\tan^2\frac A2+2\tan\frac A2\tan\frac C2-1=0$. Prove that (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i).
questions.answer: Proved: each of (i), (ii), (iii) is equivalent to $A=B$, so (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i)
questions.key_idea: Every condition reduces to $A=B$; for (iii) use $xy+yz+zx=1$ for the half-angle tangents, which makes (iii) factor as $(x-y)(x+z)=0$.
solution: (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii): $\frac a{\cos A}=\frac b{\cos B}\Rightarrow a\cos B=b\cos A$.
Cosine rule: $a\cdot\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2ac}=b\cdot\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}\Rightarrow a^2+c^2-b^2=b^2+c^2-a^2$, so $a=b$ and $A=B$.
Then $C=\pi-2A$ and $2\sin A\cos B=2\sin A\cos A=\sin2A=\sin(\pi-2A)=\sin C$: (ii) holds.
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii): $\sin C=\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B$, so (ii) gives $\sin A\cos B=\cos A\sin B$, i.e. $\sin(A-B)=0$; as $|A-B|<\pi$, $A=B$ and $C=\pi-2A$.
Then $\frac C2=\frac\pi2-A$ and $\tan\frac C2=\cot A=\frac{1-\tan^2\frac A2}{2\tan\frac A2}$.
Substitute: $\tan^2\frac A2+2\tan\frac A2\cdot\frac{1-\tan^2\frac A2}{2\tan\frac A2}-1=\tan^2\frac A2+1-\tan^2\frac A2-1=0$: (iii) holds.
(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i): let $x=\tan\frac A2$, $y=\tan\frac B2$, $z=\tan\frac C2$; in every triangle $xy+yz+zx=1$.
(iii) reads $x^2+2xz=1=xy+yz+zx$, so $x^2+xz-xy-yz=0$, i.e. $(x-y)(x+z)=0$. As $x+z>0$, $x=y$, so $A=B$.
Then $a=b$ (sine rule) and $\cos A=\cos B$, hence $\frac a{\cos A}=\frac b{\cos B}$: (i) holds. So (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i).
questions.correction_note: The PDF proves (i) => (ii) (via a = b, A = B), but its step for (ii) and for (iii) both start from the already derived A = B and C = pi - 2A instead of from (ii) itself, the working stops mid-line at an unsimplified expression, and the implication (iii) => (i) is not shown at all. A complete chain was written: (ii) => (iii) derives A = B from (ii); (iii) => (i) is added using xy + yz + zx = 1.

alternate_solutions.idea: Show each of (i), (ii), (iii) is separately equivalent to $A=B$; then the cycle of implications follows at once.
solution: (i): by the sine rule $\frac a{\cos A}=\frac b{\cos B}\iff\frac{\sin A}{\cos A}=\frac{\sin B}{\cos B}\iff\tan A=\tan B$. Two angles of a triangle with the same tangent are equal, so (i) $\iff A=B$ (if $A=B$ both are acute, so (i) is defined and true).
(ii): $2\sin A\cos B=\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B\iff\sin(A-B)=0\iff A=B$.
(iii): with $x,y,z$ the half-angle tangents, $xy+yz+zx=1$ turns (iii) into $(x-y)(x+z)=0\iff x=y\iff A=B$.
Hence (i) $\iff$ (ii) $\iff$ (iii) $\iff A=B$, which contains (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i).

useful_results: In every triangle $\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2+\tan\frac B2\tan\frac C2+\tan\frac C2\tan\frac A2=1$; conditions such as $x^2+2xz=1$ then factor as $(x-y)(x+z)=0$.
$2\sin A\cos B=\sin C\iff\sin(A-B)=0\iff A=B$ - a one-line test for an isosceles triangle with $a=b$.
$a\cos B=b\cos A\iff\sin(A-B)=0\iff a=b$; more generally $a\cos A=b\cos B$ holds iff $a=b$ or $C=90^\circ$.

concepts: Ambiguous case (SSA): cosine rule and number of triangles
Area of a triangle
questions.question: Two sides of a triangle are of lengths $\sqrt6$ and $4$ and the angle opposite to the smaller side is $30^\circ$. How many such triangles are possible? Find the length of their third side and area.
questions.answer: Two triangles: third side $2\sqrt3+\sqrt2$ or $2\sqrt3-\sqrt2$; areas $\left(2\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)$ and $\left(2\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)$ sq. units respectively
questions.key_idea: The cosine rule on the $30^\circ$ angle gives a quadratic for the third side; two positive roots mean two triangles.
solution: The sides are $\sqrt6$ and $4$ with $\sqrt6<4$, so $30^\circ$ is the angle opposite $\sqrt6$. Let the third side be $a$.
Cosine rule: $\cos30^\circ=\frac{a^2+16-6}{2a\cdot4}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
$a=\frac{4\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{48-4\cdot1\cdot10}}2=\frac{4\sqrt3\pm2\sqrt2}2=2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2$.
Both roots are positive, so two triangles are possible, with third side $2\sqrt3+\sqrt2$ or $2\sqrt3-\sqrt2$.
The angle $30^\circ$ lies between the sides $4$ and $a$, so area $=\frac12\cdot4\cdot a\sin30^\circ=a$: the areas are $2\sqrt3+\sqrt2$ and $2\sqrt3-\sqrt2$ sq. units.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working ends at the two values of the third side; it never shows the area that its answer line quotes. The last step (area = 1/2 * 4 * a * sin 30 degrees = a) was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Sine rule first: $\sin C=\sqrt{\frac23}<1$ gives an acute and an obtuse $C$, hence two triangles; the third side follows from $b=2R\sin B$.
solution: With $A=30^\circ$ opposite $\sqrt6$ and $C$ opposite $4$: $\frac{\sqrt6}{\sin30^\circ}=\frac4{\sin C}\Rightarrow\sin C=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\frac23}$.

$\sin C<1$, and $4>\sqrt6$ so $C>30^\circ$ is allowed in both forms: $\cos C=\pm\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (acute $C\approx54.7^\circ$ or obtuse $C\approx125.3^\circ$, and $A+C<180^\circ$ in both). Two triangles.
$2R=\frac{\sqrt6}{\sin30^\circ}=2\sqrt6$ and $\sin B=\sin(A+C)=\frac12\cos C+\frac{\sqrt3}2\sin C=\pm\frac1{2\sqrt3}+\frac{\sqrt2}2$.
Third side $=2R\sin B=2\sqrt6\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2\pm\frac1{2\sqrt3}\right)=2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot4\cdot(\text{third side})\cdot\sin30^\circ=2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2$.

useful_results: SSA: given angle $\theta$ opposite side $x$ and another side $y$, two triangles exist iff $y\sin\theta<x<y$; here $4\sin30^\circ=2<\sqrt6<4$.
The third side $t$ satisfies $t^2-2yt\cos\theta+y^2-x^2=0$; its two roots are positive when $x<y$ (product $y^2-x^2>0$) and the discriminant $4\left(x^2-y^2\sin^2\theta\right)>0$.
When the angle lies between $y$ and $t$, area $=\frac12yt\sin\theta$; here $\frac12\cdot4\cdot\frac12\cdot t=t$ so area equals the third side.

concepts: Areas of inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons
G.M. and H.M. relations
questions.question: With reference to a given circle, $A_1$ and $B_1$ are the areas of the inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons of $n$ sides, $A_2$ and $B_2$ are corresponding quantities for regular polygons of $2n$ sides. Prove that: (1) $A_2$ is a geometric mean between $A_1$ and $B_1$; (2) $B_2$ is a harmonic mean between $A_2$ and $B_1$.
questions.key_idea: With $\theta=\frac\pi n$: $A_1=\frac n2R^2\sin2\theta$, $B_1=nR^2\tan\theta$, and halving $\theta$ gives $A_2,B_2$.
solution: Let the circle have radius $R$. Each side of the inscribed regular $n$-gon subtends $\frac{2\pi}n$ at the centre: $A_1=\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$.
The circumscribed $n$-gon splits into $2n$ right triangles with legs $R$ and $R\tan\frac\pi n$: $B_1=nR^2\tan\frac\pi n$.
Replacing $n$ by $2n$: $A_2=nR^2\sin\frac\pi n$ and $B_2=2nR^2\tan\frac\pi{2n}$.
(1) $A_1B_1=\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n\cdot nR^2\tan\frac\pi n=n^2R^4\sin^2\frac\pi n=A_2^2$, so $A_2=\sqrt{A_1B_1}$ is the G.M. of $A_1$ and $B_1$.
(2) $\frac1{A_2}+\frac1{B_1}=\frac1{nR^2\sin\frac\pi n}+\frac{\cos\frac\pi n}{nR^2\sin\frac\pi n}=\frac{1+\cos\frac\pi n}{nR^2\sin\frac\pi n}$.
$=\frac{2\cos^2\frac\pi{2n}}{nR^2\cdot2\sin\frac\pi{2n}\cos\frac\pi{2n}}=\frac1{nR^2\tan\frac\pi{2n}}=\frac2{B_2}$.
So $\frac2{B_2}=\frac1{A_2}+\frac1{B_1}$: $B_2$ is the harmonic mean of $A_2$ and $B_1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes B_2 = 2nR^2 tan(2*pi/n); replacing n by 2n in B_1 = nR^2 tan(pi/n) gives 2nR^2 tan(pi/(2n)) (the PDF's last line already uses tan(pi/2n)). Corrected; the formulas for A_1 and B_1, which the PDF takes from its figure, are written out in one line each.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express everything through $B_1$ and $\cos\theta$: $A_2=B_1\cos\theta$, $A_1=A_2\cos\theta$ and $B_2=B_1(1-t^2)$ with $t=\tan\frac\theta2$.
solution: Put $\theta=\frac\pi n$. $B_1=nR^2\tan\theta$, $A_2=nR^2\sin\theta=B_1\cos\theta$ and $A_1=nR^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=A_2\cos\theta$.
$B_2=2nR^2\tan\frac\theta2$; with $t=\tan\frac\theta2$, $\tan\theta=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}$, so $\frac{B_2}{B_1}=\frac{2t}{\tan\theta}=1-t^2$.
(2) H.M. of $A_2$ and $B_1$ $=\frac{2A_2B_1}{A_2+B_1}=\frac{2B_1\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$, and with $\cos\theta=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, $1+\cos\theta=\frac2{1+t^2}$ this equals $B_1(1-t^2)=B_2$.

useful_results: For a circle of radius $R$: inscribed regular $n$-gon area $\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$, circumscribed $nR^2\tan\frac\pi n$; their ratio is $\cos^2\frac\pi n$.
Doubling the number of sides: $A_{2n}=\sqrt{A_nB_n}$ and $B_{2n}=\frac{2A_{2n}B_n}{A_{2n}+B_n}$ - Archimedes' recurrences for approximating $\pi$.
Numerical check ($n=4$, $R=1$): $A_1=2$, $B_1=4$, $A_2=2\sqrt2=\sqrt8$ and $B_2=8\tan22.5^\circ\approx3.3137=\frac{2\cdot2.8284\cdot4}{2.8284+4}$.

concepts: Right triangle: circumradius, exradius and half-angle trigonometry
questions.question: The triangle $ABC$ is a right angled triangle, right angle at $A$. The ratio of the radius of the circle circumscribed to the radius of the circle escribed to the hypotenuse is $\sqrt2:\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)$. Find the acute angles $B$ and $C$. Also find the ratio of the two sides of the triangle other than the hypotenuse.
questions.key_idea: For a right angle at $A$: $r_a=R(1+\sin B+\cos B)$, so the given ratio fixes $\sin B+\cos B=\sqrt{\frac32}$.
solution: Right angle at $A$: the hypotenuse is $a=2R$, $b=2R\sin B$ and $c=2R\sin C=2R\cos B$.
Exradius to the hypotenuse: $r_a=\frac{\Delta}{s-a}$ with $\Delta=\frac12bc=2R^2\sin B\cos B$ and $s-a=R(\sin B+\cos B-1)$.
$r_a=\frac{2R^2\sin B\cos B}{R(\sin B+\cos B-1)}=R\cdot\frac{(\sin B+\cos B)^2-1}{\sin B+\cos B-1}=R(\sin B+\cos B+1)$.
Given $\frac R{r_a}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3+\sqrt2}$: $\sin B+\cos B+1=\frac{\sqrt3+\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt{\frac32}+1$.
$\sin B+\cos B=\sqrt{\frac32}$, i.e. $\sqrt2\sin\left(B+\frac\pi4\right)=\frac{\sqrt6}2$, so $\sin\left(B+\frac\pi4\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
$B+\frac\pi4=\frac\pi3$ or $\frac{2\pi}3$ (as $0<B<\frac\pi2$): $B=\frac\pi{12}$ or $B=\frac{5\pi}{12}$.
Take $B=\frac{5\pi}{12}$; then $C=\frac\pi2-B=\frac\pi{12}$ (the other choice just swaps $B$ and $C$).
$\frac bc=\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}=\frac{\sin75^\circ}{\sin15^\circ}=\tan75^\circ=2+\sqrt3$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF uses r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2), which is the INRADIUS, not the radius of the escribed circle to the hypotenuse (r_a = 4R sin(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2)); its later sign steps then produce cos(B + pi/4) = -sqrt3/2. For the stated ratio the inradius version has no solution (it needs sin B + cos B = 2 + sqrt(3/2) > sqrt2). The working was rewritten with the exradius. The PDF's final answer B = 5pi/12, C = pi/12, b/c = 2 + sqrt3 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a right angle at $A$, $r_a=s$; the given ratio gives $b+c$, and then $b,c$ are the roots of a quadratic.
solution: Take $R=1$: hypotenuse $a=2$ and $b^2+c^2=4$. For a right angle at $A$, $s(s-a)=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}4=\frac{bc}2=\Delta$, so $r_a=\frac\Delta{s-a}=s$.
$\frac R{r_a}=\frac1s=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3+\sqrt2}$ gives $s=\sqrt{\frac32}+1$, so $b+c=2s-a=\sqrt6$.
$bc=\frac{(b+c)^2-(b^2+c^2)}2=\frac{6-4}2=1$, so $b,c$ are roots of $t^2-\sqrt6t+1=0$: $t=\frac{\sqrt6\pm\sqrt2}2$.
$\frac bc=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}=\frac{(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2}4=\frac{8+2\sqrt{12}}4=2+\sqrt3$.
$\sin B=\frac b2=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}4=\sin75^\circ$, so $B=\frac{5\pi}{12}$ and $C=\frac\pi{12}$.

useful_results: Right angle at $A$: $r_a=s$, $r=s-a$ and $\Delta=s(s-a)=(s-b)(s-c)$.
Exradius $r_a=4R\sin\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2$ versus inradius $r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$ - read which circle the question names.
For a right triangle $\frac R{r_a}=\frac a{2s}=\frac1{1+\sin B+\cos B}$, and $\sin B+\cos B=\frac{b+c}a$.

concepts: Circles touching two sides and the incircle: tangent lengths and half-angle tangents
questions.question: $ABC$ is a triangle. Circles are drawn inside the triangle at the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ with radii $r_1=1$, $r_2=4$, $r_3=9$ respectively, each touching two sides of the triangle and the incircle. Find the radius of the incircle of $\triangle ABC$.
questions.key_idea: A circle of radius $\rho$ in the angle $A$ touching both sides and the incircle gives $\tan\frac A2=\frac{r-\rho}{2\sqrt{r\rho}}$; then $\sum\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2=1$.
solution: Let $r$ be the inradius. The incircle and the circle of radius $1$ at $A$ touch side $AB$ and each other externally, so the segment between their points of contact $X$, $F$ on $AB$ is $XF=\sqrt{(r+1)^2-(r-1)^2}=2\sqrt r$.
Similarly for radius $4$ at $B$: $YF=\sqrt{(r+4)^2-(r-4)^2}=4\sqrt r$, and for radius $9$ at $C$ the segment is $6\sqrt r$.
The line of centres at $A$ is the bisector of $\angle A$, inclined at $\frac A2$ to $AB$; the right triangle with legs $r-1$ and $2\sqrt r$ gives $\tan\frac A2=\frac{r-1}{2\sqrt r}$.
Similarly $\tan\frac B2=\frac{r-4}{4\sqrt r}$ and $\tan\frac C2=\frac{r-9}{6\sqrt r}$.
Since $\frac A2+\frac B2+\frac C2=\frac\pi2$: $\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2+\tan\frac B2\tan\frac C2+\tan\frac C2\tan\frac A2=1$.
$\frac{(r-1)(r-4)}{2\sqrt r\cdot4\sqrt r}+\frac{(r-4)(r-9)}{4\sqrt r\cdot6\sqrt r}+\frac{(r-9)(r-1)}{6\sqrt r\cdot2\sqrt r}=1$.
$(r-11)(r-1)=0$. The incircle must be larger than the circles at the vertices ($r>9$), so $r=1$ is rejected and $r=11$.
questions.correction_note: After 'Multiplying it throughout by 24r' the PDF has the middle term as (r - 9)(r - 9); it should be (r - 4)(r - 9) (from tan(B/2) tan(C/2)). It also prints '6r^2 = 72r + 66 = 0' for 6r^2 - 72r + 66 = 0. Corrected; the quadratic r^2 - 12r + 11 = 0 and the answer r = 11 are the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Heron's formula in the form $r^2(x+y+z)=xyz$ for the tangent lengths $x=r\cot\frac A2$, $y=r\cot\frac B2$, $z=r\cot\frac C2$.
solution: Let $x=s-a$, $y=s-b$, $z=s-c$ be the tangent lengths from $A,B,C$ to the incircle. Then $x+y+z=s$ and $\Delta=rs$, so Heron's formula $\Delta^2=s\,xyz$ becomes $r^2(x+y+z)=xyz$.
With $\tan\frac A2=\frac{r-1}{2\sqrt r}$ etc.: $x=r\cot\frac A2=\frac{2r\sqrt r}{r-1}$, $y=\frac{4r\sqrt r}{r-4}$, $z=\frac{6r\sqrt r}{r-9}$.
$r^2(x+y+z)=xyz$ becomes, after dividing by $2r^{7/2}$: $\frac1{r-1}+\frac2{r-4}+\frac3{r-9}=\frac{24r}{(r-1)(r-4)(r-9)}$.

useful_results: A circle of radius $\rho$ placed in the angle $A$ touching both sides and the incircle (radius $r$) satisfies $\sin\frac A2=\frac{r-\rho}{r+\rho}$, hence $\tan\frac A2=\frac{r-\rho}{2\sqrt{r\rho}}$.
In every triangle $\sum\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2=1$ and $\sum\cot\frac A2=\prod\cot\frac A2$; the half-angles add to $\frac\pi2$.
Check: $r=11$ gives $\sin\frac A2=\frac56$, $\sin\frac B2=\frac7{15}$, $\sin\frac C2=\frac1{10}$, and $\sin^2\frac A2+\sin^2\frac B2+\sin^2\frac C2+2\prod\sin\frac A2=1$.

concepts: Incircle and tangent lengths: $PB\cdot PC=(s-b)(s-c)$
Power of a point and tangents to a circle
questions.question: Line $l$ is a tangent to a unit circle $S$ at a point $P$. Point $A$ and the circle $S$ are on the same side of $l$, and the distance from $A$ to $l$ is $3$. Two tangents from point $A$ intersect line $l$ at the points $B$ and $C$ respectively. Find the value of $(PB)(PC)$.
questions.key_idea: $S$ is the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ ($r=1$, altitude $3$), so $PB\cdot PC=(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{r^2s}{s-a}=3$, whatever the position of $A$.
solution: As in the PDF's figure take $A$ on the line through $P$ perpendicular to $l$ (the symmetric position; the alternate shows the answer does not depend on this). Then $AP=3$ and the diameter through $P$ ends at $P_1$ with $AP_1=3-2=1$.
Power of the point $A$: $AP\times AP_1=AR^2$, where $R$ is the point of contact of a tangent from $A$. So $3\times1=AR^2$ and $AR=\sqrt3$.
In the right triangle formed by $A$, the centre and $R$ (radius $1$, tangent length $\sqrt3$): $\tan\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, so $\theta=30^\circ$ and $\angle A=2\theta=60^\circ$.
In the right triangle $APB$ (right angle at $P$): $PB=AP\tan30^\circ=3\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$; by symmetry $PC=\sqrt3$.
$(PB)(PC)=\left(\sqrt3\right)^2=3$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's figure and working place A directly above P (the symmetric position) without saying so; the question only fixes the distance of A from l. The value 3 holds for every position of A on the parallel line (proved in the alternate and checked numerically for several positions), so the answer is unchanged; the assumption is now stated.

alternate_solutions.idea: $S$ is the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ with $r=1$ and altitude $h_a=3$; $PB=s-b$, $PC=s-c$ and Heron's formula give the product for any position of $A$.
solution: $S$ touches the line $BC=l$ at $P$ and the lines $AB$, $AC$, and lies on the same side of $BC$ as $A$: it is the incircle of $\triangle ABC$, with $r=1$ and contact point $P$ on $BC$.
Tangent lengths: $PB=s-b$ and $PC=s-c$.
$\Delta=rs=s$ and $\Delta=\frac12a\cdot3$, so $a=\frac{2s}3$ and $s-a=\frac s3$.
Heron: $\Delta^2=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$, so $s^2=s\cdot\frac s3\cdot(s-b)(s-c)$.
Hence $(PB)(PC)=(s-b)(s-c)=3$, for every position of $A$ on the line parallel to $l$.

useful_results: The incircle touches $BC$ at $P$ with $BP=s-b$, $PC=s-c$; therefore $PB\cdot PC=(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{r^2s}{s-a}$ (from $r^2=\frac{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}s$).
Equivalent form: $(s-b)(s-c)=\Delta\tan\frac A2$; here $\Delta=s$ and $\tan\frac A2=\frac3s$.

With the radius $r$ and the altitude $h$ from $A$ fixed, $a=\frac{2rs}h$, so $s-a=s\left(1-\frac{2r}h\right)$ and $(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{r^2}{1-\frac{2r}h}=\frac{r^2h}{h-2r}$ - here $\frac{3}{3-2}=3$ - independent of where $A$ moves along the parallel line.

concepts: Orthocentre distances: $AH=2R\cos A$, $HD=2R\cos B\cos C$
Identity $\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C$
questions.question: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocentre $H$. $D,E,F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $A,B,C$ on the opposite sides. $R$ is the circumradius of $\triangle ABC$. Given $(AH)(BH)(CH)=3$ and $(AH)^2+(BH)^2+(CH)^2=7$, find (a) the ratio $\frac{\prod\cos A}{\sum\cos^2A}$, (b) the product $(HD)(HE)(HF)$, (c) the value of $R$.
questions.key_idea: $AH=2R\cos A$ turns both given conditions into $8R^3\prod\cos A=3$ and $4R^2\sum\cos^2A=7$; the identity $\sum\cos^2A=1-2\prod\cos A$ then gives $R$.
solution: From the right triangle $BDH$: $BD=c\cos B$ and $\angle BHD=C$, so $BH=\frac{c\cos B}{\sin C}=2R\cos B$; similarly $AH=2R\cos A$ and $CH=2R\cos C$.
$(AH)(BH)(CH)=3\Rightarrow(2R)^3\cos A\cos B\cos C=3$ ...(1)
$AH^2+BH^2+CH^2=7\Rightarrow4R^2\left[\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C\right]=7$ ...(2)
(a) (1) $\div$ (2): $\frac{8R^3\prod\cos A}{4R^2\sum\cos^2A}=\frac37$, so $\frac{\prod\cos A}{\sum\cos^2A}=\frac3{14R}$.
(b) $HD=BD\cot C=\frac{c\cos B\cos C}{\sin C}=2R\cos B\cos C$; similarly $HE=2R\cos C\cos A$ and $HF=2R\cos A\cos B$.
$(HD)(HE)(HF)=8R^3\cos^2A\cos^2B\cos^2C=8R^3\left[\frac3{8R^3}\right]^2=\frac9{8R^3}$, using (1).
(c) $\cos^2A+\cos^2B=1+\cos(A+B)\cos(A-B)$ and $\cos C=-\cos(A+B)$, so $\sum\cos^2A=1+\cos(A+B)\left[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)\right]=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C$.
Then (a) $=\frac3{14\cdot\frac32}=\frac17$ and (b) $=\frac9{8\cdot\frac{27}8}=\frac13$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at the equation 7/(4R^2) = 1 - 6/(8R^3) and states R = 3/2 in the answer line without solving the cubic 4R^3 - 7R - 3 = 0 (roots 3/2, -1/2, -1), and it does not give the numerical values of (a) and (b). These steps were added; the expressions 3/(14R) and 9/(8R^3) and R = 3/2 are the PDF's. A triangle with these data exists (angles about 66.1, 48.2 and 65.7 degrees, all acute).

alternate_solutions.idea: For (b): $HD=\frac{BH\cdot CH}{2R}$, so the product of the three small segments follows from the given product $AH\cdot BH\cdot CH$ without any cosines.
solution: $BH=2R\cos B$ and $CH=2R\cos C$, so $HD=2R\cos B\cos C=\frac{BH\cdot CH}{2R}$; likewise $HE=\frac{CH\cdot AH}{2R}$ and $HF=\frac{AH\cdot BH}{2R}$.
$(HD)(HE)(HF)=\frac{(AH\cdot BH\cdot CH)^2}{(2R)^3}=\frac{3^2}{8R^3}=\frac9{8R^3}$ directly from the given product.
With $R=\frac32$ (from the main solution) this is $\frac{9}{8\cdot\frac{27}8}=\frac13$.

useful_results: Orthocentre distances in an acute triangle: $AH=2R\cos A$, $HD=2R\cos B\cos C$, and $AH\cdot HD=BH\cdot HE=CH\cdot HF=4R^2\cos A\cos B\cos C$ (power of $H$).
$\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C$ whenever $A+B+C=\pi$.
$AH^2+BH^2+CH^2=12R^2-\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)$; check with a unit equilateral triangle: $R=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, sum $=1=4-3$.

concepts: Heron's formula and A.M.-G.M. inequality (Ravi substitution)
questions.question: If $\Delta$ is the area of a triangle with side lengths $a,b,c$, then show that $\Delta\le\frac14\sqrt{(a+b+c)abc}$. Also show that equality occurs in the above inequality if and only if $a=b=c$.
questions.key_idea: Heron's formula reduces the claim to $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\le\frac{abc}8$, which is $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\ge8xyz$ for $x=s-a$ etc.
solution: To prove: $16\Delta^2\le2s\cdot abc$, where $2s=a+b+c$. By Heron, $16\Delta^2=16s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$, so it suffices to show $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\le\frac{abc}8$.
Let $s-a=x$, $s-b=y$, $s-c=z$ (all positive). Then $x+y=c$, $y+z=a$, $z+x=b$.
A.M. $\ge$ G.M.: $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ ...(i), $y+z\ge2\sqrt{yz}$ ...(ii), $z+x\ge2\sqrt{zx}$ ...(iii).
Multiplying (i), (ii), (iii) (all sides positive): $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\ge8xyz$, i.e. $abc\ge8(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$.
So $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\le\frac{abc}8$ and $16\Delta^2=16s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\le16s\cdot\frac{abc}8=2s\cdot abc=(a+b+c)abc$.
Taking square roots, $\Delta\le\frac14\sqrt{(a+b+c)abc}$.
Equality holds iff equality holds in each of (i)-(iii), i.e. $x=y=z$, i.e. $s-a=s-b=s-c$, which means $a=b=c$.
Conversely for an equilateral triangle of side $a$: $\Delta=\frac{\sqrt3}4a^2$ and $\frac14\sqrt{3a\cdot a^3}=\frac{\sqrt3}4a^2$, so equality holds.
questions.correction_note: The PDF proves (s-a)(s-b)(s-c) <= abc/8 and stops there: it does not carry the result back to the required inequality through Heron's formula and does not treat the equality case that the question asks for. Those two parts (steps 5-8) were added; the Ravi substitution and the A.M.-G.M. product are the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: With $\Delta=rs$ and $abc=4R\Delta$ the inequality is exactly Euler's $R\ge2r$.
solution: $abc=4R\Delta$ and $a+b+c=2s$, so $(a+b+c)abc=8Rs\Delta$.
$16\Delta^2\le8Rs\Delta\iff2\Delta\le Rs\iff2rs\le Rs\iff R\ge2r$, using $\Delta=rs$.
Euler: $OI^2=R^2-2Rr\ge0$, hence $R\ge2r$, so the inequality holds.
Equality iff $OI=0$, i.e. the incentre coincides with the circumcentre, which happens exactly for the equilateral triangle: $a=b=c$.

useful_results: Ravi substitution $x=s-a$, $y=s-b$, $z=s-c$ ($a=y+z$, etc.) turns triangle problems into inequalities in positive reals; $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\ge8xyz$ is the one used here.
$abc\ge8(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\iff R\ge2r$ (Euler), since $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{\Delta^2}s$ and $abc=4R\Delta$; equality iff equilateral.
Related bound: $\Delta\le\frac{(a+b+c)^2}{12\sqrt3}$ (isoperimetric inequality for triangles), equality for the equilateral triangle.

concepts: Areas of inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons
Double-angle identities
questions.question: If $I_n$ is the area of the $n$-sided regular polygon inscribed in a circle of unit radius and $O_n$ is the area of the polygon circumscribing the given circle, prove that $I_n=\frac{O_n}2\left(1+\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2I_n}n\right)^2}\right)$.
questions.key_idea: With $\theta=\frac\pi n$: $I_n=\frac n2\sin2\theta$ and $O_n=n\tan\theta$, so $\frac{I_n}{O_n}=\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}2$.
solution: Let $\theta=\frac\pi n$. The inscribed regular $n$-gon in the unit circle splits into $n$ isosceles triangles with equal sides $1$ and apex angle $2\theta$: $I_n=\frac n2\sin2\theta$ (the PDF's hint).
The circumscribed regular $n$-gon has apothem $1$ and splits into $2n$ right triangles with legs $1$ and $\tan\theta$: $O_n=n\tan\theta$ (the PDF's hint).
From the first, $\frac{2I_n}n=\sin2\theta$, so $\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2I_n}n\right)^2}=\sqrt{1-\sin^22\theta}=|\cos2\theta|=\cos2\theta$ for $n\ge4$ (then $2\theta\le\frac\pi2$).
Right side: $\frac{O_n}2(1+\cos2\theta)=\frac n2\tan\theta\cdot2\cos^2\theta=n\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac n2\sin2\theta=I_n$.
Hence $I_n=\frac{O_n}2\left(1+\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2I_n}n\right)^2}\right)$, valid for $n\ge4$.
(For $n=3$, $\cos2\theta=-\frac12<0$ and the square root equals $-\cos2\theta$, so the formula fails: $I_3\approx1.299$ but the right side is $\approx3.897$.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF gives only the hint 'put I_n = (n/2) sin(2*pi/n) and O_n = n tan(pi/n)'; the complete proof was written. The identity needs cos(2*pi/n) >= 0, i.e. n >= 4 (for n = 3 the square root equals |cos 120 deg| = -cos 120 deg and the statement is false); the question does not state this restriction.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two regular $n$-gons are similar, so the ratio of their areas is the square of the ratio of their circumradii: $I_n=O_n\cos^2\frac\pi n$.
solution: The inscribed polygon has circumradius $1$; the circumscribed polygon has apothem $1$, hence circumradius $\sec\frac\pi n$.
Similar polygons: $\frac{I_n}{O_n}=\left(\frac1{\sec\frac\pi n}\right)^2=\cos^2\frac\pi n=\frac{1+\cos\frac{2\pi}n}2$.
The inscribed area is $I_n=\frac n2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$, so $\sin\frac{2\pi}n=\frac{2I_n}n$ and (for $n\ge4$, $\cos\frac{2\pi}n\ge0$) $\cos\frac{2\pi}n=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2I_n}n\right)^2}$.
Therefore $I_n=\frac{O_n}2\left(1+\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2I_n}n\right)^2}\right)$.

useful_results: Regular $n$-gon of circumradius $R$: area $\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$; of inradius $r$: area $nr^2\tan\frac\pi n$.
Inscribed-to-circumscribed area ratio for the same circle is $\cos^2\frac\pi n$ (similar polygons with circumradius ratio $\cos\frac\pi n$); for $n=4$ it is $\frac12$.
Sign check: $\sqrt{1-\sin^2x}=|\cos x|$, so write $\cos x$ only after confirming $\cos x\ge0$ - here this requires $n\ge4$.

concepts: Altitudes of a triangle and the sine rule
questions.paragraph: Consider a triangle $ABC$, where $x,y,z$ are the lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the vertices of the triangle to the opposite sides $a,b,c$ respectively; let the letters $R,r,s,\Delta$ denote the circumradius, inradius, semi-perimeter and area of the triangle respectively.
questions.question: If $\frac{bx}c+\frac{cy}a+\frac{az}b=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}k$, then the value of $k$ is:
questions.key_idea: An altitude is a side times a sine ($\frac xc=\sin B$ etc.), so the sum becomes $\sum a\sin A=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{2R}$.
solution: $\frac{bx}c+\frac{cy}a+\frac{az}b=b\cdot\frac xc+c\cdot\frac ya+a\cdot\frac zb$.
$x$ is the perpendicular from $A$ on $BC$, so in the right triangle on side $c$: $\sin B=\frac xc$. Similarly $\sin C=\frac ya$ and $\sin A=\frac zb$.
So the sum is $b\sin B+c\sin C+a\sin A$.
Sine rule $\sin A=\frac a{2R}$, $\sin B=\frac b{2R}$, $\sin C=\frac c{2R}$: the sum is $b\cdot\frac b{2R}+c\cdot\frac c{2R}+a\cdot\frac a{2R}=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{2R}$.
Comparing with $\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}k$: $k=2R$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace each altitude by $\frac{2\Delta}{\text{side}}$ and use $abc=4R\Delta$.
solution: $x=\frac{2\Delta}a$, $y=\frac{2\Delta}b$, $z=\frac{2\Delta}c$.
$\frac{bx}c=\frac{2\Delta b}{ac}=\frac{2\Delta b^2}{abc}$, and similarly $\frac{cy}a=\frac{2\Delta c^2}{abc}$, $\frac{az}b=\frac{2\Delta a^2}{abc}$.
Sum $=\frac{2\Delta\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)}{abc}=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{2R}$, since $abc=4R\Delta$.
Hence $k=2R$.

useful_results: The altitude from $A$ is $x=b\sin C=c\sin B=\frac{2\Delta}a$; each altitude has two expressions through sines and one through the area.
$\sum a\sin A=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{2R}$ (sine rule $\sin A=\frac a{2R}$).
$abc=4R\Delta$ turns any expression symmetric in the sides into one in $R$ and $\Delta$.

concepts: Cotangent sum and altitudes of a triangle
questions.paragraph: Consider a triangle $ABC$, where $x,y,z$ are the lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the vertices of the triangle to the opposite sides $a,b,c$ respectively; let the letters $R,r,s,\Delta$ denote the circumradius, inradius, semi-perimeter and area of the triangle respectively.
questions.question: If $\cot A+\cot B+\cot C=k\left(\frac1{x^2}+\frac1{y^2}+\frac1{z^2}\right)$, then the value of $k$ is:
questions.key_idea: Both sums reduce to a multiple of $a^2+b^2+c^2$: $\sum\cot A=\frac R{abc}\sum a^2$ and $\sum\frac1{x^2}=\frac{4R^2}{a^2b^2c^2}\sum a^2$.
solution: $\cot A=\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\frac{2R\cos A}a$.

$\cot A+\cot B+\cot C=2R\left[\frac{\cos A}a+\frac{\cos B}b+\frac{\cos C}c\right]=2R\left[\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2abc}+\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2abc}+\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2abc}\right]=\frac R{abc}\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)$.
$\sin B=\frac xc=\frac b{2R}\Rightarrow x=\frac{bc}{2R}$, so $\frac1x=\frac{2R}{bc}$. Similarly $\frac1y=\frac{2R}{ac}$ and $\frac1z=\frac{2R}{ab}$.
$\frac1{x^2}+\frac1{y^2}+\frac1{z^2}=\frac{4R^2}{a^2b^2c^2}\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)$.
So $\frac R{abc}\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)=k\cdot\frac{4R^2}{a^2b^2c^2}\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)$.
$k=\frac{abc}{4R}=\Delta$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use areas: $\cot A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}$ and $x=\frac{2\Delta}a$, so both sides share the factor $a^2+b^2+c^2$.
solution: $\frac1{x^2}=\frac{a^2}{4\Delta^2}$, so $\frac1{x^2}+\frac1{y^2}+\frac1{z^2}=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta^2}$.
Dividing: $k=\frac{\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta}}{\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta^2}}=\Delta$, option (C).

useful_results: $\cot A+\cot B+\cot C=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta}$ in every triangle.
Altitudes: $x=\frac{2\Delta}a$, so $\frac1x:\frac1y:\frac1z=a:b:c$ and $\sum\frac1{x^2}=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta^2}$.

Hence $\frac{\sum\cot A}{\sum\frac1{x^2}}=\Delta$ for every triangle; check on an equilateral triangle of side $2$: $\sum\cot A=3\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$, each altitude is $\sqrt3$ so $\sum\frac1{x^2}=1$, and $\Delta=\sqrt3$.

concepts: Altitudes of a triangle: two expressions for each altitude
questions.paragraph: Consider a triangle $ABC$, where $x,y,z$ are the lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the vertices of the triangle to the opposite sides $a,b,c$ respectively; let the letters $R,r,s,\Delta$ denote the circumradius, inradius, semi-perimeter and area of the triangle respectively.
questions.question: The value of $\frac{c\sin B+b\sin C}x+\frac{a\sin C+c\sin A}y+\frac{b\sin A+a\sin B}z$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Each altitude equals a side times a sine in two ways: $c\sin B=b\sin C=x$, so every fraction equals $2$.
solution: The perpendicular from $A$ on $BC$ is $x=c\sin B=b\sin C$.
Adding: $\frac{c\sin B+b\sin C}x=\frac{2x}x=2$ ...(i)
Similarly $a\sin C=c\sin A=y$, so $\frac{a\sin C+c\sin A}y=2$ ...(ii)
And $b\sin A=a\sin B=z$, so $\frac{b\sin A+a\sin B}z=2$ ...(iii)
Adding (i), (ii) and (iii): the value is $6$, option (D).
useful_results: Each altitude has two side-times-sine expressions: $x=b\sin C=c\sin B$, $y=c\sin A=a\sin C$, $z=a\sin B=b\sin A$ (the sine rule in disguise).
So $\frac{c\sin B+b\sin C}x=2$ identically; recognise such sums as $2$ before computing anything.
Quick check on an equilateral triangle of side $a$: $x=\frac{\sqrt3}2a$ and $\frac{2a\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2}{\frac{\sqrt3}2a}=2$ for each term, total $6$.

concepts: Angles in A.P. and exterior-angle theorem
Circumcircle of a right triangle
questions.paragraph: An altitude $BD$ and a bisector $BE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ from the vertex $B$. It is known that the length of side $AC=1$, and the magnitudes of the angles $BEC$, $ABD$, $ABE$, $BAC$ form an arithmetic progression.
questions.question: The area of the circle circumscribing $\triangle ABC$ is:
questions.key_idea: Write the four A.P. angles symmetrically, use $\angle BEC=\angle BAE+\angle ABE$ and $\angle ABD=90^\circ-A$ to find the triangle: $30^\circ$-$90^\circ$-$60^\circ$.
solution: The angles $\angle BEC$, $\angle ABD$, $\angle ABE$, $\angle BAC$ are in A.P. Let $\angle BEC=\alpha-3\beta$, $\angle ABD=\alpha-\beta$, $\angle ABE=\alpha+\beta$, $\angle BAC=\alpha+3\beta$.
Exterior angle theorem in $\triangle ABE$: $\angle BEC=\angle BAE+\angle ABE$, so $\alpha-3\beta=(\alpha+3\beta)+(\alpha+\beta)$.
This gives $\alpha=-7\beta$.
In the right triangle $ABD$ ($\angle ADB=90^\circ$): $\angle ABD+\angle BAD=\frac\pi2$, so $(\alpha-\beta)+(\alpha+3\beta)=\frac\pi2$, i.e. $2\alpha+2\beta=\frac\pi2$ and $\alpha+\beta=\frac\pi4$.
With $\alpha=-7\beta$: $-6\beta=\frac\pi4$, so $\beta=-\frac\pi{24}$ and $\alpha=\frac{7\pi}{24}$.

$\angle B=2\angle ABE=2(\alpha+\beta)=\frac\pi2$ (as $BE$ bisects $\angle B$), $\angle A=\alpha+3\beta=\frac\pi6$ and $\angle C=\frac\pi3$: $\triangle ABC$ is a $30^\circ$-$90^\circ$-$60^\circ$ triangle.
$\angle B=90^\circ$, so $AC=1$ is a diameter of the circumcircle: radius $\frac12$ and area $\pi\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac\pi4$, option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\angle ABD=90^\circ-A$ directly: with $A=x$ and $\angle ABE=y$ the four angles are $x+y,\ 90^\circ-x,\ y,\ x$, and the A.P. conditions are two linear equations.
solution: Let $\angle BAC=x$ and $\angle ABE=y$. In the right triangle $ABD$, $\angle ABD=90^\circ-x$; the exterior angle at $E$ gives $\angle BEC=x+y$.
In the stated order the angles are $x+y,\ 90^\circ-x,\ y,\ x$, in A.P.
The last three terms: $2y=(90^\circ-x)+x=90^\circ$, so $y=45^\circ$.
The first three terms: $2(90^\circ-x)=(x+y)+y=x+90^\circ$, so $180^\circ-2x=x+90^\circ$ and $x=30^\circ$.
$\angle B=2y=90^\circ$, $\angle A=30^\circ$, $\angle C=60^\circ$; the hypotenuse $AC=1$ is the circumdiameter, so the area is $\frac\pi4$.

useful_results: Angles in A.P.: use the symmetric form $\alpha-3\beta,\alpha-\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha+3\beta$ (common difference $2\beta$), or equivalently two 'twice the middle' equations.
In $\triangle ABD$ with $BD\perp AC$: $\angle ABD=90^\circ-\angle A$; the exterior angle of $\triangle ABE$ at $E$ is $\angle A+\angle ABE$.
A right angle at $B$ makes the hypotenuse $AC$ the circumdiameter: $R=\frac{AC}2$, area $=\frac\pi4AC^2$.

concepts: Circumcentre of a right triangle and inradius of an equilateral triangle
questions.paragraph: An altitude $BD$ and a bisector $BE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ from the vertex $B$. It is known that the length of side $AC=1$, and the magnitudes of the angles $BEC$, $ABD$, $ABE$, $BAC$ form an arithmetic progression.
questions.question: Let $O$ be the circumcentre of $\triangle ABC$. The radius of the circle inscribed in $\triangle BOC$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\triangle ABC$ is right-angled at $B$, so $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $\triangle BOC$ is equilateral with side $\frac12$.
solution: From Q26: $\angle B=90^\circ$, $\angle A=30^\circ$, $\angle C=60^\circ$ and $AC=1$, so $AB=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $BC=\frac12$.
The circumcentre $O$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AC$, so $OB=OC=\frac12$; with $\angle C=60^\circ$, $\triangle BOC$ is equilateral with side $\frac12$.
Inradius $r=\frac\Delta s$: $\Delta=\frac{\sqrt3}4\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac{\sqrt3}{16}$ and $s=\frac12\cdot\frac32=\frac34$.
$r=\frac{\sqrt3/16}{3/4}=\frac{\sqrt3}{12}=\frac1{4\sqrt3}$, option (B).
useful_results: The circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse; so $OB=OC=\frac{AC}2$ and $\triangle BOC$ is isosceles with base angle $=\angle C$ (equilateral when $C=60^\circ$).
Inradius of an equilateral triangle of side $t$: $r=\frac{\sqrt3}6t=\frac t{2\sqrt3}$; here $t=\frac12$ gives $\frac1{4\sqrt3}$.
$r=\frac\Delta s$ holds for every triangle.

concepts: Reflection of a point in a line and altitude of a right triangle
questions.paragraph: An altitude $BD$ and a bisector $BE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ from the vertex $B$. It is known that the length of side $AC=1$, and the magnitudes of the angles $BEC$, $ABD$, $ABE$, $BAC$ form an arithmetic progression.
questions.question: Let $B'$ be the image of point $B$ with respect to side $AC$ of $\triangle ABC$. Then the length $BB'$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $BB'=2BD$, with $BD$ the distance from $B$ to $AC$; in the equilateral $\triangle BOC$, $BD=OB\sin60^\circ$.
solution: From Q26: $\triangle ABC$ has $\angle B=90^\circ$, $\angle A=30^\circ$, $\angle C=60^\circ$ and $AC=1$.
$O$ is the midpoint of $AC$, so $OB=OC=\frac12$ and $\triangle BOC$ is equilateral with side $\frac12$; hence $\angle BOD=\angle BOC=\frac\pi3$.
In the right triangle $BOD$ (with $D$ the foot of the altitude from $B$): $BD=OB\sin\frac\pi3=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{\sqrt3}4$.
$B'$ is the mirror image of $B$ in $AC$, so $BB'=2BD=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: The distance from $B$ to the hypotenuse is $\frac{AB\cdot BC}{AC}$ (two expressions for the area).
solution: With $\angle B=90^\circ$: $AB=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $BC=\frac12$, $AC=1$.
Area $=\frac12AB\cdot BC=\frac12AC\cdot BD$, so $BD=\frac{AB\cdot BC}{AC}=\frac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\frac12=\frac{\sqrt3}4$.
$BB'=2BD=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, option (D).

useful_results: The reflection of $B$ in a line is at distance $2\times$ (distance of $B$ from the line): $BB'=2h_b=\frac{4\Delta}{b}$.
Altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle: $h=\frac{pq}{\text{hyp}}$ (legs $p,q$); here $\frac{\frac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\frac12}1=\frac{\sqrt3}4$.
Equivalent: $h=\frac{AC}2\sin(\angle BOC)$ with $O$ the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

concepts: Half-angle formulas and Napier's analogy
Inequalities for the tangents of the angles of a triangle
questions.question:
Match the following columns.
Column I: (A) In a $\triangle ABC$, $(a+b+c)(b+c-a)=\lambda bc$, where $\lambda\in I$; then the greatest value of $\lambda$ is. (B) In a $\triangle ABC$, $\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=9$. If $\tan^2A+\tan^2B+\tan^2C=k$, then the least value of $k$ satisfying this is. (C) In a triangle $ABC$ the line joining the circumcentre to the incentre is parallel to $BC$; then the value of $\cos B+\cos C$ is. (D) If in a $\triangle ABC$, $a=5$, $b=4$ and $\cos(A-B)=\frac{31}{32}$, then the side $c$ is equal to.
Column II: (P) $3$ (Q) $9(3)^{1/3}$ (R) $1$ (S) $6$
questions.answer: (A) P; (B) Q as keyed (the AM-GM bound; it is not actually attained, see note); (C) R; (D) S
questions.key_idea: Each item is a one-step identity: $\lambda=2+2\cos A$, $\sum\tan=\prod\tan$ with A.M.-G.M., $R\cos A=r$, and Napier's analogy.
solution: (A) $(a+b+c)(b+c-a)=\lambda bc\Rightarrow(b+c)^2-a^2=\lambda bc\Rightarrow b^2+c^2-a^2=-2bc+\lambda bc$.
So $2\cos A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{bc}=\lambda-2$, i.e. $\lambda=2+2\cos A$. As $A\in(0,\pi)$, $0<\lambda<4$; the integer values are $1,2,3$ and the greatest is $3$: (P).
(B) $A+B+C=\pi\Rightarrow\tan(A+B+C)=0\Rightarrow\tan A+\tan B+(1-\tan A\tan B)\tan C=0$, so $\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C=9$.
A.M.-G.M. on the squares: $\frac{\tan^2A+\tan^2B+\tan^2C}3\ge\left(\tan^2A\tan^2B\tan^2C\right)^{1/3}=81^{1/3}$, so $k\ge3\cdot3^{4/3}=9\cdot3^{1/3}$: the keyed match is (Q).
(C) $OI\parallel BC$ means $O$ and $I$ are at the same distance from $BC$: $R\cos A=r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$.
Using $r=R(\cos A+\cos B+\cos C-1)$: $\cos A=\cos A+\cos B+\cos C-1$, so $\cos B+\cos C=1$: (R).
(D) $2\cos^2\frac{A-B}2-1=\frac{31}{32}\Rightarrow\cos^2\frac{A-B}2=\frac{63}{64}$, so $\cos\frac{A-B}2=\frac{\sqrt{63}}8$ and $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac1{\sqrt{63}}$.
Napier's analogy: $\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2=\frac19\cot\frac C2=\frac1{\sqrt{63}}$, so $\cot\frac C2=\frac3{\sqrt7}$, $\tan\frac C2=\frac{\sqrt7}3$ and $\cos\frac C2=\frac34$.
$\cos C=2\cos^2\frac C2-1=\frac98-1=\frac18$. Cosine rule: $\frac18=\frac{25+16-c^2}{2\cdot4\cdot5}$, so $c^2=36$ and $c=6$: (S).
questions.correction_note: (A) The PDF writes cos A = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/(bc) = lambda - 2 (the factor 2 is missing; it is 2cos A) and then takes cos A = 1 'to get lambda = 3'; cos A = 1 is impossible in a triangle. Correct: 2cos A = lambda - 2 lies in (-2, 2), so 0 < lambda < 4 and the greatest integer lambda is 3 (answer unchanged). (B) The key B -> Q is the A.M.-G.M. bound 9*3^(1/3) = 12.98, but it is NOT the least value of k: equality would need tan A = tan B = tan C = t with 3t = t^3 = 9, which is impossible. The stronger QM-AM bound gives k >= 81/3 = 27, and the actual minimum (two equal tangents, 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 9 = 0, t = 4.251) is about 36.39, which is not in Column II. So the question itself is flawed; the keyed match B -> Q is the bound the PDF derives. (D) The relation sign printed between tan((A-B)/2) and 1/sqrt63 in the PDF is garbled; it is an equality.

alternate_solutions.idea: Different tools: (A) half-angle formula $\lambda=4\cos^2\frac A2$; (B) QM-AM shows the keyed bound is not sharp; (D) Mollweide's formulas.
solution: (A) $(a+b+c)(b+c-a)=2s\cdot2(s-a)=4s(s-a)$ and $\cos^2\frac A2=\frac{s(s-a)}{bc}$, so $\lambda=4\cos^2\frac A2\in(0,4)$; the greatest integer is $3$ (P).

(B) By QM-AM, $\sum\tan^2A\ge\frac{\left(\sum\tan A\right)^2}3=27$, which already exceeds the keyed value $9\cdot3^{1/3}\approx12.98$. So $9\cdot3^{1/3}$ is only a lower bound; it is never attained because equal tangents $t$ would need $3t=t^3=9$. The true minimum (two equal tangents, $t\approx4.251$) is $\approx36.39$.

(D) Mollweide: $\frac{a-b}c=\frac{\sin\frac{A-B}2}{\cos\frac C2}$ and $\frac{a+b}c=\frac{\cos\frac{A-B}2}{\sin\frac C2}$, with $\sin\frac{A-B}2=\sqrt{\frac{1-31/32}2}=\frac18$ and $\cos\frac{A-B}2=\frac{\sqrt{63}}8$.

$\frac1c=\frac{1/8}{\cos\frac C2}$ gives $c=8\cos\frac C2$; $\frac9c=\frac{\sqrt{63}/8}{\sin\frac C2}$ gives $c=\frac{72}{\sqrt{63}}\sin\frac C2$. Equating, $\tan\frac C2=\frac{\sqrt{63}}9=\frac{\sqrt7}3$, so $\cos\frac C2=\frac34$ and $c=6$ (S).

useful_results: $(a+b+c)(b+c-a)=4bc\cos^2\frac A2$, i.e. $\lambda=2(1+\cos A)\in(0,4)$.

If $A+B+C=\pi$ then $\sum\tan A=\prod\tan A$. With the sum fixed, QM-AM ($\sum\tan^2A\ge\frac{(\sum\tan A)^2}3$) is always at least as strong as A.M.-G.M. on the squares, because $\sum\tan A\ge3\sqrt3$ in any triangle.
$OI\parallel BC\iff R\cos A=r\iff\cos B+\cos C=1$ (from $\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=1+\frac rR$).
Napier / Mollweide: $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2$ gives the third side from two sides and $\cos(A-B)$.

concepts: Circles touching externally: distances between centres and right triangles
Radical axis and common tangents
questions.question:
Consider two circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ having their centres at $B$ and $C$ with radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively, touching each other externally. A circle $S$ with radius $r$ and centre at $A$ touches both of them externally.
Column I: (A) If $\triangle ABC$ is right angled at $A$, then $\frac{r_2+r}{r_2-r}$ is. (B) If $\triangle ABC$ is right angled at $A$ and $r_1r_2=3+2\sqrt2$, then. (C) If the common tangent of $S_1$ and $S_2$ at their point of contact passes through the centre of circle $S$, then. (D) If $r_1=r_2=R$ and the circles $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S$ have the same external common tangent, then $r$ is.
Column II: (P) $r\ge1$ (Q) $r_1=r_2$ (R) $\frac R4$ (S) $\frac{r_1}r$
questions.answer: (A) S; (B) P as keyed (but the correct relation is $r\le1$, so no listed option is right, see note); (C) Q; (D) R
questions.key_idea: Right angle at $A$ with $AB=r+r_1$, $AC=r+r_2$, $BC=r_1+r_2$ gives $r_1r_2=r\left(r+r_1+r_2\right)$; for a common tangent line, contact points are $2\sqrt{\rho_1\rho_2}$ apart.
solution: (A) $AB=r+r_1$, $AC=r+r_2$, $BC=r_1+r_2$. With the right angle at $A$: $(r_1+r_2)^2=(r+r_1)^2+(r+r_2)^2$.

(B) $r_1r_2=3+2\sqrt2=\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2=p$. From (A): $r^2+r(r_1+r_2)-r_1r_2=0$, so $r=\frac{-m+\sqrt{m^2+4p}}2=\frac{2p}{m+\sqrt{m^2+4p}}$ where $m=r_1+r_2\ge2\sqrt p=2\left(\sqrt2+1\right)$ (A.M.-G.M.).
$r$ DEcreases as $m$ increases, so it is largest at the least $m=2\left(\sqrt2+1\right)$ (i.e. $r_1=r_2$): $r\le\frac{2p}{2\sqrt p+\sqrt{8p}}=\frac{\sqrt p}{1+\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{\sqrt2+1}=1$.
So $r\le1$, with $r=1$ only when $r_1=r_2=\sqrt2+1$ (for example $r_1=1$, $r_2=3+2\sqrt2$ gives $r\approx0.77$). The keyed (P) '$r\ge1$' is therefore not correct.
(C) The common tangent at the point of contact of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is their radical axis; $A$ lies on it, so its tangent lengths to $S_1$ and $S_2$ are equal: $AB^2-r_1^2=AC^2-r_2^2$.
$(r+r_1)^2-r_1^2=(r+r_2)^2-r_2^2\Rightarrow r^2+2rr_1=r^2+2rr_2\Rightarrow r_1=r_2$: (Q).

(D) Let $S_1$, $S_2$, $S$ (radii $r_1=r_2=R$ and $r$) touch the same line. Two touching circles of radii $\rho_1,\rho_2$ touching a line have their contact points $2\sqrt{\rho_1\rho_2}$ apart: $S_1,S_2$ are $2R$ apart, $S_1,S$ are $2\sqrt{Rr}$ apart and $S,S_2$ are $2\sqrt{Rr}$ apart.

$S$ lies between: $2\sqrt{Rr}+2\sqrt{Rr}=2R\Rightarrow\sqrt r=\frac{\sqrt R}2$, so $r=\frac R4$: (R). (In general $\frac1{\sqrt r}=\frac1{\sqrt{r_1}}+\frac1{\sqrt{r_2}}$, i.e. $r=\frac{r_1r_2}{\left(\sqrt{r_1}+\sqrt{r_2}\right)^2}$, as in the PDF.)
questions.correction_note: (B) The PDF replaces r1 + r2 by its minimum 2(sqrt2+1) inside r = [-(r1+r2) + sqrt((r1+r2)^2 + 4 r1 r2)]/2 and concludes r >= 1. But r decreases as r1 + r2 grows, so the minimum of r1 + r2 gives the MAXIMUM of r: r <= 1, with equality only when r1 = r2. The statement 'r >= 1' (option P) is therefore false in general, and the key B -> P is wrong (the correct statement would be r <= 1; none of the listed options expresses it). (C) The PDF's circle-property step 'AE x AB = AD^2' is rewritten as the equal-tangent-length (radical axis) argument; same result. (D) is the PDF's result with the working shortened to the contact-point lengths. (A) is as in the PDF.

alternate_solutions.idea: (B) Parametrise $r_1+r_2=2(\sqrt2+1)\cosh t$ to see $r\le1$ at once; (D) Descartes' circle theorem with the line as a circle of curvature $0$.
solution: (B) With $p=r_1r_2=\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2$ write $r_1+r_2=2\sqrt p\cosh t$ ($t\ge0$). Then $r=\frac{2p}{m+\sqrt{m^2+4p}}=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{\cosh t+\sqrt{\cosh^2t+1}}$.
The denominator is at least $1+\sqrt2$ (its value at $t=0$) and grows with $t$, so $r\le\frac{\sqrt2+1}{1+\sqrt2}=1$, with equality only at $t=0$, i.e. $r_1=r_2$. Hence $r\le1$, not $r\ge1$.
(D) Descartes' theorem for two mutually tangent circles and a line tangent to both, plus a third circle in the gap: $k=k_1+k_2+2\sqrt{k_1k_2}$ with curvatures $k=\frac1\rho$.

Three mutually tangent circles with centres $A,B,C$ have a triangle with sides $r+r_1$, $r+r_2$, $r_1+r_2$; the semi-perimeter is $r+r_1+r_2$ and the area is $\sqrt{rr_1r_2(r+r_1+r_2)}$ (right angle at $A$ gives $r_1r_2=r(r+r_1+r_2)$).

questions.question:
$ABC$ is a triangle in which $\cos(A-B)=\frac45$ and $BC=6$, $AC=3$. $AD$ is the median through $A$, $\angle BAD=\alpha$, $CL$ is perpendicular to $AD$.
Column I: (A) The value of $\sin\alpha$ is. (B) The length of the median $AD$ is. (C) The radius of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ is. (D) The value of $\cot\angle ADC$ is.
Column II: (P) $\frac{3\sqrt5}2$ (Q) $\frac1{\sqrt{10}}$ (R) $3\sqrt2$ (S) $1$
questions.key_idea: Napier's analogy with $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac13$ gives $\cot\frac C2=1$, so $C=90^\circ$; then every item is a right-triangle computation.
solution: $2\cos^2\frac{A-B}2-1=\frac45\Rightarrow\cos^2\frac{A-B}2=\frac9{10}$, so $\cos\frac{A-B}2=\frac3{\sqrt{10}}$ and $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac13$.
Napier's analogy with $a=BC=6$, $b=AC=3$: $\tan\frac{A-B}2=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2$, so $\frac13=\frac39\cot\frac C2$ and $\cot\frac C2=1$, so $C=\frac\pi2$.
$\triangle ABC$ is right-angled at $C$ with $CA=3$, $CB=6$ and $AB=\sqrt{36+9}=3\sqrt5$; $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $CD=BD=3$.
(B) $AD=\sqrt{AC^2+CD^2}=\sqrt{9+9}=3\sqrt2$: (R).

(A) $\sin B=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac3{3\sqrt5}=\frac1{\sqrt5}$. In $\triangle ABD$ the sine rule gives $\frac{BD}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{AD}{\sin B}$, i.e. $\frac3{\sin\alpha}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{1/\sqrt5}$, so $\sin\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}$: (Q).
(C) $2R=\frac b{\sin B}=\frac3{1/\sqrt5}=3\sqrt5$, so $R=\frac{3\sqrt5}2$: (P).
(D) In the right triangle $ADC$: $\cot\angle ADC=\frac{CD}{AC}=\frac33=1$: (S).

alternate_solutions.idea: Get $C=90^\circ$ from $\sin A=2\sin B$ and $\tan A\tan B=1$ (no Napier), then use coordinates for every item.
solution: $A>B$ since $a>b$; put $A=B+\delta$ with $\cos\delta=\frac45$, $\sin\delta=\frac35$. The sine rule gives $\sin A=\frac ab\sin B=2\sin B$.
$\frac45\sin B+\frac35\cos B=2\sin B\Rightarrow\tan B=\frac12$, so $\tan A=\tan(B+\delta)=\frac{\frac12+\frac34}{1-\frac38}=2$; $\tan A\tan B=1$ gives $C=90^\circ$.
Coordinates: $C=(0,0)$, $B=(6,0)$, $A=(0,3)$, $D=(3,0)$. Then $AD=\sqrt{9+9}=3\sqrt2$ (B) and $\cot\angle ADC=\frac{CD}{CA}=1$ (D).
The circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so $R=\frac{AB}2=\frac{3\sqrt5}2$ (C).
With $\vec{AB}=(6,-3)$ and $\vec{AD}=(3,-3)$: $\sin\alpha=\frac{|6(-3)-(-3)(3)|}{3\sqrt5\cdot3\sqrt2}=\frac9{9\sqrt{10}}=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}$ (A).
